name: Exclamation
pattern: Utterance with exclamatory prosody and heightened-stance force

entry.name: Exclamation
entry.pattern: Utterance with exclamatory prosody and heightened-stance force

dimensions.form: Realized by interjections, exclamative clauses, extra-clausal NPs, or prosodically marked declaratives
dimensions.meaning: Heightened speaker stance toward a referent, situation, or degree
dimensions.function: Expressive force; stands alone as a complete utterance
dimensions.distribution: Utterance-level; resists syntactic integration and at-issue challenge

1.definition: An utterance-level force category, expressing heightened speaker stance with exclamatory prosody
1.details: Terminology: exclamative is the clause type (syntactic), exclamatory the property of uses, exclamation the utterance-level force category (pragmatic). This entry is a Constructionary pragmatic profile, not a claim that CGEL recognizes a unified grammatical class: CGEL p. 923 treats exclamation as structurally nebulous and samples several formally distinct realizations. Membership here is graded: interjections are the prototype; exclamative clauses are core; directive-ostensive NPs are prototypically members; vocatives enter only via the summons/call use; declaratives join by prosody alone (That's amazing!). The category cross-cuts ostensive-np-001 rather than containing it: tag vocatives are structural-yes/force-no, while exclamatory declaratives are force-yes/structural-no.

examples.note: Interjection; the prototype (pure force, no discourse referent)
Non-headed construction with exclamative clausal semantics; cf. the headed Clause What a lovely day it is!

constraints.description: Not at-issue; the force resists direct denial (That's false cannot target the exclamatory stance).
Exclamatory prosody is non-reducible; deaccenting removes membership.

projection.target: Locating an utterance in the exclamation profile predicts stand-alone viability, non-reducible exclamatory prosody, heightened-stance interpretation, and resistance to at-issue denial, across formally unrelated realizations
projection.evidence: The projections hold from interjections through exclamative clauses to recruited declaratives; the profile is realizationally promiscuous but functionally uniform

stabilisers.evidence: Need to express heightened stance rapidly, without clausal assembly

known_boundary_items: CGEL does not posit a well-defined grammatical class of non-exclamative exclamations; this entry proposes a cross-form pragmatic profile
tag and address vocatives (structural profile without exclamatory force)
exclamatory declaratives (force without the extra-clausal structure)

curious.title: Short bursts of strong feeling
curious.summary: An exclamation is an utterance that expresses strong feeling, and the way it's said is part of what makes it one.
curious.body: Ouch! is the clearest exclamation. It's a complete utterance on its own and it just expresses feeling. But the category is wider than that. What a lovely day! and A snake! can be exclamations too, and so can an ordinary-looking statement like That's amazing! What these share is an exclamatory tone of voice and a heightened feeling. With Ouch! that is pure feeling; with the others it is directed at something. Take away the tone and the exclamation goes with it. The feeling also can't be argued with in the usual way: replying That's false doesn't target the feeling expressed. This dictionary treats exclamation as a pattern of use, and notes that the grammar book it draws on doesn't recognize it as one tidy class.
curious.try: Say That's amazing in a flat voice, then say it as if you've just seen something astonishing. Which one is an exclamation?

teacher.summary: Helps separate exclamation (a use of language with a heightened-stance tone) from exclamative (a clause type).
teacher.explain: This dictionary offers a pragmatic profile, not a claim that CGEL recognizes a unified grammatical class; CGEL treats exclamation as structurally nebulous. Exclamation is an utterance-level force: heightened speaker stance with exclamatory prosody, complete on its own. Realizations vary. Interjections are the prototype, exclamative clauses are core, directive-ostensive NPs are prototypical members, vocatives qualify only as summons or calls, and a declarative joins through prosody alone (That's amazing!). Keep three terms apart: exclamative is a clause type, exclamatory describes uses, exclamation is the force category. The stance isn't at-issue, so it resists direct denial.
teacher.terms: Interjection is the traditional name for words like Ouch. Exclamative clause is the clause type.
watch_for: A learner might treat the exclamation mark as the whole test, when the core properties in this dictionary include exclamatory prosody.
A learner might use exclamation and exclamative as one word, though exclamative names a clause type and exclamation a use.
A learner might expect That's false to answer the stance in That's amazing!, though the force resists direct denial.
teacher.activity: Students say That's amazing three ways (flat, bored, astonished) and vote on which are exclamations. Then they look at Ouch, What a lovely day and A snake, note that each is a complete utterance said with feeling, and note how differently they're built.

child.hook: How do you say That's amazing when you are really amazed?
child.explain: An exclamation shows a big feeling. How you say it matters. Ouch! and A snake! are exclamations. So is That's amazing! if you say it with feeling.
child.play: Say That's amazing like a sleepy robot. Now say it like you just saw a rocket. Only one is an exclamation. Which?
